title: THE SEXUAL SCANDAL PAUL SAID EVEN THE PAGANS WOULDN’T TOLERATE
paragraphs: THE SEXUAL SCANDAL PAUL SAID EVEN THE PAGANS WOULDN’T TOLERATE

The terrifying part of 1 Corinthians 5 isn’t simply what one man did in secret. It’s what an entire church learned to tolerate in public—and what Paul did next reveals the difference between grace that saves and “grace” that quietly lets sin destroy us.
There are passages in the Bible we love to underline.
There are passages we put on coffee mugs.
There are passages we whisper when we cannot sleep.
And then there are passages like 1 Corinthians 5.
Passages that walk into the room, turn on the light, and expose what everyone hoped would remain comfortably hidden.
Paul had heard something about the church in Corinth.
Something sexual.
Something public.
Something so disturbing that the apostle did not soften his opening sentence with pleasantries.
He wrote:
“Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία…”
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you…”
Then Paul makes the accusation even more devastating.
“…καὶ τοιαύτη πορνεία ἥτις οὐδὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν…”
…kai toiautē porneia hētis oude en tois ethnesin…
Sexual immorality of such a kind that it was not even found among the Gentiles.
And then Paul names it.
“…ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.”
A man had his father’s wife.
—1 Corinthians 5:1
Read that again.
Slowly.
Paul was writing to Christians.
Not to a pagan temple.
Not to a Roman brothel.
Not to people who had never heard the Gospel.
To the church.
And somewhere inside that congregation was a man involved with his father’s wife.

The language strongly indicates a relationship with his stepmother or a woman who was his father’s wife. Whatever the precise surrounding circumstances, the relationship itself was explicitly forbidden by Scripture. Leviticus 18:8 had already declared that a man must not uncover the nakedness of his father’s wife.
Paul’s shock was therefore not difficult to understand.
But here is where the passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because the sexual scandal was not the only scandal.
The church’s reaction was another.
“And you are arrogant!”
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 5:2.
Imagine expecting sympathy and receiving that sentence.
Imagine Paul walking into the congregation while everybody is discussing the sinful man and saying, in effect:
Why are all of you acting as though he is the only problem?
That changes everything.
Because Paul’s deepest confrontation was not merely directed toward a sexually immoral individual.
He confronted a spiritually complacent church.
They knew.
And somehow they had learned to live with what they knew.
That may be the part of this chapter modern Christians desperately need to hear.
We have become remarkably skilled at being horrified by everybody else’s sin while negotiating private treaties with our own.
We condemn what disgusts us.
We rationalize what attracts us.
We can recognize rebellion immediately when someone else commits it, yet when our own desires are involved, suddenly everything becomes complicated.
“It’s just a struggle.”
“God understands.”
“We love each other.”
“Nobody knows.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“It isn’t hurting anybody.”
“I prayed about it.”
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
He does.
And that should comfort the repentant sinner.
But it should terrify the person determined to keep hiding.
Because God knows the heart beneath the explanation.
He knows whether you are fighting sin or feeding it.
He knows whether you stumbled and are crawling back toward Him—or whether you have decorated your chains and renamed them freedom.
He knows.
The Greek word Paul uses is πορνεία—porneia.
It is the word commonly translated “sexual immorality.”
Paul does not treat sexual sin as an embarrassing little imperfection Christians should simply stop talking about.
Neither does he treat sexually broken people as disposable human beings.
That distinction matters enormously.
Biblical Christianity does not require us to choose between truth and compassion.
Jesus gives us both.
Truth without grace can become cruelty.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
But Jesus Christ came “full of grace and truth.”
And some of us need both desperately tonight.
Because maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody found the messages.
Nobody discovered the browser history.
Nobody knows about the relationship.
Nobody knows what happens when you are alone.
Nobody knows about the emotional affair you keep insisting is only friendship.
Nobody knows what you watch after your family goes to sleep.
Nobody knows the person you become behind a locked screen.
Nobody knows the memory you keep revisiting.
Nobody knows how many times you promised God, “This is the last time.”
Nobody knows.
Except God.
And perhaps reading that makes your stomach tighten.
Perhaps you expected another article about some ancient Corinthian pervert and suddenly realized Scripture has turned the mirror around.
That is what the Word of God does.
We approach it intending to examine the text.
Then the text examines us.
And please hear this carefully:
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation says, “Run away from God. You are filthy.”
Conviction says, “Run toward God. You cannot keep living like this.”
The enemy wants your shame to become a hiding place.
Jesus wants your conviction to become a doorway home.
That is why Paul’s response in 1 Corinthians 5 sounds so severe.
He commands the church to deal decisively with the man’s open, unrepentant sin.
Modern ears sometimes recoil at that.
Where is the compassion?
Where is the mercy?
Where is grace?
Look closer.
Grace is precisely why Paul refuses to pretend nothing is wrong.
If someone you love is walking toward destruction, silence is not necessarily kindness.
Sometimes silence is cowardice wearing the clothes of compassion.
Paul even describes the disciplinary action as having a redemptive purpose: “…so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.”
That changes the emotional temperature of the entire chapter.
The goal was not humiliation for entertainment.
Not revenge.
Not gossip.
Not religious superiority.
Not, “Look how disgusting this man is.”
The goal was salvation.
Restoration.
Awakening.
Repentance.
Paul was willing to make the man uncomfortable because eternity mattered more than maintaining appearances.
And perhaps that is where some churches have failed.
Some churches have failed by becoming harsh places where broken people are publicly crushed.
Others have failed in the opposite direction—becoming places where almost nothing can be confronted because confrontation itself is considered unloving.
Paul allows neither extreme.
The church must not delight in exposing sinners.
But neither may the church celebrate, normalize, protect, or casually tolerate unrepentant sin among those professing Christ.
Why?
Paul gives an unforgettable picture.
“A little leaven leavens the whole lump.”
Sin rarely remains neatly contained.
What we tolerate begins teaching us.
What we repeatedly excuse begins reshaping our conscience.
What once made us blush eventually makes us shrug.
What once made us repent eventually becomes something we defend.
And one of the most dangerous moments in your spiritual life is not necessarily when you fall.
It may be when falling no longer bothers you.
When prayer becomes quieter.
When conviction becomes easier to dismiss.
When Scripture becomes something you avoid because you already know what it will say.
When worship continues from your mouth while surrender quietly disappears from your life.
That is dangerous.
Because Christianity was never meant to become sophisticated sin management.
Jesus did not die so we could become more comfortable inside the prison.
He came to bring prisoners out.
Paul eventually writes in the next chapter:
Not negotiate with it.
Not schedule it.
Not keep it available for difficult nights.
Not follow it secretly while posting Bible verses publicly.
Flee.
There are moments when victory looks remarkably unspiritual.
Delete the number.
End the affair.
Block the account.
Confess to a trustworthy mature believer.
Move the computer.
Stop entering the environment where you repeatedly fall.
Tell your spouse the truth where appropriate and seek wise pastoral or professional help.
Get accountability.
Stop calling bondage “privacy.”
Stop calling lust “love.”
Stop calling secrecy “protection.”
Stop waiting for temptation to become weaker while continuing to feed it.
Run.
Because Jesus is better than what is killing you.
And this is where the scandal in Corinth becomes something breathtaking.
Paul does not end the Corinthian story with sexual sinners being beyond redemption.
In 1 Corinthians 6, immediately after naming sins that characterized people outside God’s kingdom, Paul tells the believers something astonishing:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That single word carries an ocean of grace.
Some of them had been sexually immoral.
Some idolaters.
Some adulterers.
Some thieves.
Some greedy.
Some drunkards.
Some revilers.
Some swindlers.
Paul does not say those histories were imaginary.
He says those histories were no longer their identity.
“And such were some of you.”
Then comes the Gospel:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for avoiding scandal.
Dead people being made alive.
Guilty people being justified.
Dirty people being washed.
Captives being liberated.
Prodigals coming home.
Sinners receiving mercy they could never purchase.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross proves your sin was so serious that the Son of God gave His life for sinners.
But the resurrection declares something equally glorious:
Your sin does not get the final word when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your story.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere beneath the respectable version of yourself is something you desperately wish could be rewritten.
A sexual past.
An abortion.
An affair.
Pornography.
Promiscuity.
A betrayal.
A secret relationship.
Years of lust.
Something done to you.
Something done by you.
A marriage you damaged.
A family you wounded.
A promise you broke.
A season you would erase if heaven allowed editing.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend it never happened.
The Gospel announces that Jesus can write something after it.
That is grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
There was something after the denial.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
There was something after the accusation.
The thief was dying beside Christ with nothing left to offer.
There was something after the criminal record.
Paul himself had persecuted the church.
There was something after the violence.
The cross stands forever as God’s declaration that your worst chapter does not possess sovereign authority over the ending.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But do not misunderstand what “rewrites” means.
Jesus does not rewrite sin by calling evil good.
He rewrites sinners by making them new.
Grace is not Jesus helping us hide the old life.
Grace is Jesus calling the old life into the grave and raising us to walk in newness of life.
That means repentance matters.
Real repentance.
Not religious embarrassment because you got caught.
Not tears because consequences arrived.
Not deleting evidence while preserving desire.
Repentance is the heart turning toward God.
It is agreeing with God about sin.
It is bringing darkness into His light.
It is abandoning the fantasy that rebellion can give us what only Christ can provide.
And sometimes repentance hurts.
Sometimes obedience costs relationships.
Sometimes confession destroys an image you spent years building.
Sometimes holiness means grieving something your flesh desperately wants.
Sometimes following Jesus feels like losing something before you understand what you are gaining.
But there is no sexual pleasure, secret relationship, hidden fantasy, applause, reputation, or temporary comfort worth trading intimacy with Christ for.
None.
Jesus is better.
Better than the fantasy.
Better than the affair.
Better than the approval.
Better than the secret.
Better than the addiction.
Better than the counterfeit intimacy.
Better than the version of yourself you are desperately trying to protect.
And if you have fallen again…
Come home.
If you have fallen fifty times…
Come home.
If you are ashamed to pray because you promised God last time would be the last time…
Come home.
Do not use grace as permission to remain in sin.
But do not let shame convince you that repentance is no longer available.
Confess.
Turn.
Seek help.
Cut off access.
Make restitution where wisdom and righteousness require it.
Walk in the light.
And believe the Gospel.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
That sentence has not expired.
Maybe the person who most needs this article is not you.
Maybe while reading, a face appeared in your mind.
Someone drifting.
Someone trapped.
Someone who still attends church but is slowly disappearing inside.
Someone whose marriage is cracking.
Someone hiding pornography.
Someone convinced that sexual sin has made them permanently filthy.
Someone who thinks God is finished with them.
Someone who needs conviction before destruction comes.
Or someone who needs grace before shame convinces them to give up.
Send this to them.
Not as a weapon.
As a rescue rope.
If something hidden was exposed while you were reading, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your life. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Or comment, “Christ is still healing me,” if your testimony is not finished yet.
Someone else may read your three words and realize they are not the only person fighting to come back into the light.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Christ, consider staying close to this ministry.
Not because supporting a ministry earns salvation—it never will.
But one genuine way believers may glorify God is by freely supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work so biblical truth can reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
But whether you ever spend a cent or not, do not leave this message without hearing the most important invitation.
Come to Jesus.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Not to merchandise.
To Jesus.
Because Paul’s scandalous chapter is ultimately not merely a warning about a man sleeping with his father’s wife.
It is a warning about what happens when sin becomes comfortable.
And it is an invitation to remember what the blood of Christ can do with people who finally stop hiding.
The Corinthian church needed truth strong enough to confront them.
The sinful man needed discipline serious enough to awaken him.
And every one of us needs grace powerful enough to save us.
Maybe your scandal never made the news.
Maybe nobody whispered your name.
Maybe your family never discovered it.
Maybe your church never knew.
Maybe your secret is still sitting safely behind a password.
But there is a far more important question than whether people know.
Does Jesus have all of you?
The room nobody enters.
The memory nobody knows.
The browser history.
The private messages.
The relationship.
The wound.
The appetite.
The shame.
The thing you keep promising to surrender tomorrow.
Does He have that too?
Because Jesus did not endure the cross merely to improve the public version of you.
He came for the person underneath it.
The real one.
The ashamed one.
The tempted one.
The guilty one.
The exhausted one.
The one still hiding.
The one reading these final words with a strange heaviness in the chest because somewhere inside, you know this stopped being an article about Corinth several paragraphs ago.
This became about you.
And perhaps tonight the Holy Spirit is not exposing you to destroy you.
Perhaps He is calling you out of the darkness because Jesus intends to heal what darkness has been consuming.
So stop running.
Stop negotiating.
Stop pretending.
Bring the scandal into the light of the cross.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Because the most unforgettable thing about your story does not have to be the night you fell.
It can be the moment Jesus found you there…and you finally stopped hiding.
And comment something honest.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“No more hiding.”
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of walking back into the light.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but once the pen is surrendered to Jesus, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
